title: Kalhana's river of kings
hookLine: a poet sits down to write the story of his valley's kings, and the first rule he sets himself is to be like a judge
carry: see it straight, free of raga and dvesha
tomorrow: why does crying at a sad play leave you lighter?
last: THE EARTH IS HOLY; WE ASK HER PARDON.

lines: A POET AND A VALLEY OF KINGS.
cards: A poet in Kashmir has a big job ahead of him. He's going to tell the story of the valley's kings, the good and the cruel, the wise and the foolish, in Sanskrit verse. Before he starts, he sets himself a rule.
A poet who tells the past, he says, deserves praise only if his words are like a judge's: free of love and free of hate. No flattery for a patron. No revenge on an enemy.
The poet's name is Kalhana. His book is the Rajatarangini, the river of kings.

teach.h: A HISTORY THAT OPENS WITH SHIVA
teach.b: Kalhana's book opens with verses honoring Shiva, then turns to the valley and tells yesterday's lake again: the water of Satisar drained and the land made ready for people.
From there it runs on, king after king, like a river. That's the picture in the title: kings rising and passing like waves on moving water. Kalhana doesn't pretend the kings were all heroes.
He tells of greed and plots and wasted lives alongside generosity and good rule. That's what his rule about the judge is for. If you love one side or hate another, you bend the story.
That pair has a name in Hindu teaching: raga and dvesha, liking and loathing. The Bhagavad Gita says the two sit waiting in everything the senses meet, and warns: don't fall under their sway.
Kalhana carries that teaching to his writing desk. He also says he read older chronicles and records and pieced them together. Then comes something a reader might not look for in a history.
Kalhana says the mood he wants the whole work to leave behind is calm: in the language of Indian poetics, the rasa of shanta, peace. Why calm, for a story full of kings?
Because if you watch power rise and fall long enough, you stop gripping it. The waves come and go. The river keeps moving.
And the rule holds for anyone telling a story about people they know: a fight between friends, a family quarrel. Before you tell it, notice where liking or loathing is leaning on the words.

how: Kalhana's Rajatarangini is read in Sanskrit and in translation as the chronicle of Kashmir's kings; Kashmiri Hindus treasure it as the valley's own story, beginning from the lake of Satisar.

games.q: two cousins argue over who ruined the family trip, and Nani asks you what really happened. you like one cousin more. by Kalhana's rule and the Gita's, what do you do?
o: tell it plainly, setting your liking aside.
go easy on the one you like; loyalty to family is dharma too.
refuse to say anything; staying out of it is detachment.
games.why: Kalhana's judge, free of love and hate, is the Gita's warning about raga and dvesha: notice them, then tell it straight.

practice: Take a pen and write one recent disagreement in a single plain sentence, as Kalhana would: what happened, and what each person did, without a word of praise or blame.
Read it back and cross out any word where liking or loathing crept in. Then let it go, like a wave on moving water.

wordCard.voice: Kashmir. The valley whose kings Kalhana set down in the Rajatarangini, the river of kings, told like a judge and meant to leave the reader calm. Today's word.

orig.note: Rajatarangini in Sanskrit, written in Devanagari: Kalhana's river of kings.

carryVoice: Take this with you: see it straight, free of raga and dvesha. Even a history of kings, here, is meant to leave you calm. More from the valley tomorrow.
